records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Iris reticulata page lists Common Name(s) Dwarf Iris, Netted Iris, Species Iris, led by Dwarf Iris. records.toxicity_detail: NC State Plant Toolbox (Iris reticulata species page): the page's Poison block is human-scoped ("Poisonous to Humans"), with Poison Severity Low (page header: "This plant has low severity poison characteristics"). Poison Symptoms as the page gives them: "CAUSES ONLY LOW TOXICITY IF EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Nausea, salivation, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, diarrhea, elevated temperature following ingestion; skin irritation upon contact with seeds, rootstock, or cell sap." Poison Toxic Principle: Pentacylic terpenoids (zeorin, missourin and missouriensin), Irisin, iridin, or irisine. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds. NC State's separate Problems tags are Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; these animal tags are separate from the human-scoped Poison block, which gives no severity for animals. NC State's Plant Type field lists Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. RHS (dedicated Iris reticulata page) says "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and "Pets: Harmful if eaten." RHS names no specific pet animal, so it is not used for toxic_to_pets. The sources differ in tone: NC State rates severity Low, while RHS says harmful if eaten with no severity rating.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Citrus x paradisi (Grapefruit), the hybrid's own page. Under the heading "Poisonous to Humans:" the page gives Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Vomiting, diarrhea, depression; potential dermatitis. The fruit is edible, skins and plant material can cause problems"; Poison Toxic Principle: Essential oils and psoralens; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. The severity rating comes from that human-scoped Poison block; the header line reads "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The page lists no poison-part list beyond the sentence that the fruit is edible while skins and plant material can cause problems. Separately, the page's Problems field carries the tags Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; those tags are not part of the Poison block and the page does not say which symptoms apply to which animal. Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems prose: "This plant can cause contact dermatitis in some people." Co-listed Plant Type values: Edible, Houseplant, Tree. Co-listed tags include #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #edible fruits #edible #houseplant #medicinal; no medicinal claims are landed. The page's Edibility field: "Fruit is eaten fresh or juiced or used to make jams, jellies or in baking." No other admissible source addresses this hybrid's toxicity. Within the page, however, the Uses (Ethnobotany) field says 'The peel is candied and used in cakes.' and 'An essential oil obtained from the peel is used as a flavoring in soft drinks, chewing gum, sweets, baked goods, ice cream.', which sits in tension with the Poison Symptoms statement that skins can cause problems and with the Essential oils toxic principle.
unknowns: Only NC State has a dedicated page for this hybrid. The RHS result found is a 'Citrus x aurantium Grapefruit Group (F)' group page (not this exact name, and it did not render text), and UF/IFAS and Clemson pages are genus-level or multi-species, so none were used. WCVP's sinking of the name into Citrus x aurantium is not from an admissible source and nothing was taken from NC State's Sour Orange page. name_note is left null because no sub-claim beyond the given/accepted name needed a note.
